c.tagline: China's hottest oasis — grapes, ruins, and the Flaming Mountains.

taxi.fareNote: City taxis are metered and Didi works in town, but the major sights are spread across the desert — most visitors hire a car with driver for the day.

emergency.note: 110 reaches police, 120 is for ambulance/medical and 119 is fire.

avoid.reason: Xinjiang — security checkpoints and surveillance; carry your passport; check advisories

hood_desc: The compact downtown hub of the oasis, with the covered bazaar, Turpan Museum, grape-trellised streets, hotels and restaurants; the walkable base most visitors stay in.

A lush vineyard gorge about 8 km northeast of town where grapes ripen under shaded trellises and cold canal water runs beside the walkways. Several manor-style hotels and family guesthouses sit inside the scenic area itself, making it a cooler, greener place to sleep than downtown.
lodging: Theme Hotel Turpan Camel Bell Winery

water.note: Drink bottled or boiled water, as is standard across China.

transit.hours: City buses run roughly 7:00 AM to 9:00 PM; taxis and Didi cover the rest, and most sights outside town need a hired car.
transit.note: Turpan is a small oasis city with local buses and taxis but no metro or in-city rail; the main sights are spread across the surrounding desert and are best reached by hired car or tour.
transit.pay: City bus fares are paid in cash or by mobile payment (Alipay/WeChat) on board (about 1-2 yuan); taxis are metered.

bus: Turpan Bus Station — coaches to Ürümqi (~2.5 h), Hami and Shanshan

car.idp: Foreign licences/IDP not valid in China — most visitors hire a car with driver

train: Turpan North Railway Station — Lanzhou–Xinjiang high-speed line, ~1 h to Ürümqi

tip.r: Tipping is not customary or expected in mainland China; there is no need to tip in restaurants or taxis.

food.name: Leghmen (laghman)
food.desc: Dough swung and stretched into long noodles by hand, then topped or stir-fried with lamb, tomato, peppers and garlic; the Uyghur everyday meal.

places.name: Guanghui Street snack zone
places.note: Main local eating strip, lined with Uyghur noodle houses and snack stalls.

places.name: Turpan Bazaar food stalls
places.note: Market kitchens pulling noodles to order beside the fruit and spice sellers.

places.name: Gaochang Road evening stalls
places.note: Night-time noodle and kebab stands used by residents rather than tour groups.

food.name: Kawap (lamb kebabs)
food.desc: Chunks of lamb alternated with fat on willow skewers, grilled over charcoal and dusted heavily with cumin, salt and chilli.

places.name: Guanghui Street snack zone
places.note: Rows of charcoal grills, the simplest and best introduction to Turpan eating.

places.name: Turpan Bazaar food stalls
places.note: Kebabs, naan and baked dumplings sold side by side in the old-city market.

places.name: Grape Valley farmhouse restaurants
places.area: Putao Gou, north of the city
places.note: Vine-shaded courtyards grilling kebabs under the trellises.

food.name: Samsa
food.desc: Square parcels of pastry filled with minced lamb, onion and black pepper, slapped onto the wall of a tandoor and baked until the shell crackles.

places.name: Turpan Bazaar food stalls
places.note: Tandoor ovens turn out samsa in batches through the morning.

places.name: Guanghui Street snack zone
places.note: Bakeries and snack windows selling samsa hot from the oven.

places.name: Grape Valley farmhouse restaurants
places.note: Village bakeries near the scenic area sell samsa and naan to visitors.

food.name: Nan (tandoor flatbread)
food.desc: Discs of bread stamped with a pattern and studded with sesame or onion, baked against the tandoor wall; the backbone of every Uyghur meal.

places.name: Turpan Bazaar bakeries
places.note: Bakers work the tandoor in the open, selling naan by the stack.

places.name: Guanghui Street snack zone
places.note: Bread ovens on the main snack street, busy from early morning.

places.name: Gaochang Road evening stalls
places.note: Evening bread stands where locals buy naan on the way home.

food.name: Polo (pilaf)
food.desc: Rice slow-cooked with lamb, carrot and onion in mutton fat until every grain is amber; served from a huge pan and eaten with pickled vegetables.

places.name: Guanghui Street snack zone
places.note: Uyghur restaurants ladle polo from the communal pan at lunchtime.

places.name: Turpan Bazaar food stalls
places.note: Market kitchens serving pilaf until the pan runs out.

places.name: Grape Valley farmhouse restaurants
places.note: Family restaurants in the vineyards serve polo with lamb and raisins.

food.name: Turpan grapes and raisins
food.desc: The Turpan basin is China grape capital; seedless green grapes are dried in latticed brick chunche sheds into raisins eaten by the handful all year.

places.name: Grape Valley (Putao Gou)
places.area: North of Turpan, at the Flaming Mountains
places.note: Vine-covered gorge where you can eat grapes under the trellises and see the drying sheds.

places.name: Turpan Bazaar
places.note: Stalls piled with dozens of raisin varieties, dried apricots and mulberries.

places.name: Guanghui Street snack zone
places.note: Fruit and grape-product shops alongside the food stalls.

food.name: Fresh grape juice
food.desc: Pressed from Turpan seedless grapes and drunk cold; in a devoutly Muslim oasis where alcohol is largely absent, this is the celebratory drink.

places.name: Grape Valley (Putao Gou)
places.note: Juice pressed on the spot in the vineyard courtyards during the harvest.

places.name: Turpan Bazaar
places.note: Juice and dried-fruit stalls through the covered market.

places.name: Guanghui Street snack zone
places.note: Cold grape and pomegranate juice sold beside the kebab grills.

food.name: Atken chay (Uyghur milk tea)
food.desc: Brick tea boiled with milk and salt, sometimes with butter or cream, poured from a metal pot and drunk with naan at breakfast and after meals.

places.name: Guanghui Street snack zone
places.note: Teahouses and breakfast shops serve the salted milk tea with fresh naan.

places.name: Turpan Bazaar teahouses
places.note: Old-city tea rooms where men sit over tea through the hottest hours.

places.name: Grape Valley farmhouse restaurants
places.note: Village households serve milk tea and dried fruit to guests under the vines.

landmarks: Emin Minaret (Sugong Ta)
China's tallest minaret, a tapering 44-metre tower of patterned sun-dried brick from 1778, rises gracefully beside its adobe mosque amid the vineyards.
Jiaohe Ancient City (Yarkhoto)
One of the world's best-preserved earthen cities crowns a river-carved island plateau, its 2,000-year-old streets, temples and dwellings hauntingly intact.
Gaochang Ancient City (Karakhoja)
The sprawling adobe ruins of a Silk Road kingdom's capital, where the monk Xuanzang preached, bake beneath the Flaming Mountains' scorched flanks.
Flaming Mountains (Huoyan Shan)
Furrowed red sandstone ridges shimmer like fire in the desert heat, immortalised in the classic tale Journey to the West as a blazing obstacle.
Turpan Karez System
Museums and open channels reveal the ingenious underground aqueducts, hand-dug over centuries, that carry Tianshan meltwater beneath the desert to Turpan's oases.
Bezeklik Thousand Buddha Caves
Buddhist grottoes painted between the 5th and 14th centuries cling to a cliff above the Murtuk River gorge, their surviving murals hauntingly beautiful.
Grape Valley (Putao Gou)
A lush ravine of trellised vineyards beneath the Flaming Mountains, where Uyghur families dry sweet seedless raisins in latticed mud-brick drying houses.
Tuyoq Village (Tuyugou)
An ancient Uyghur village of mud-brick homes and a green-tiled mosque nestles in a red canyon, flanked by vineyards and early Buddhist caves.
Astana Tombs
The desert necropolis of ancient Gaochang preserved silks, documents and naturally mummified nobles for over a millennium in its painted underground chambers.
Aydingkol Lake
The lowest point in China at 154 metres below sea level, this glittering salt-crusted lakebed marks the searing heart of the Turpan Depression.

train.note: There are no international trains from Turpan; the cross-border services to Almaty and Astana run from Urumqi, about two and a half hours away. Turpan has two stations and they are easily confused: Turpan North on the Lanzhou-Urumqi high-speed line is the closer and faster option, while the older Turpan Station is out at Daheyan, some 50 km northwest of town, and needs a connecting bus or taxi. From the conventional station, Kashgar takes about 25 hours, Korla around 8 hours, Liuyuan for Dunhuang 8-9 hours, Lanzhou about 25 hours and Xi'an 40-45 hours. Book on 12306 with your passport, and budget extra time for the airport-style security screening applied throughout Xinjiang.

bus.note: No international coaches run from Turpan. The Long Distance Bus Station on Laocheng Road has services to Urumqi in about 2.5 hours, Kumul (Hami) and Korla in 6-7 hours, Kucha in 13-14 hours and Kashgar in around 32 hours, the last being a gruelling sleeper-bus haul that the railway does considerably better. Tickets are bought at the counter with your passport, which is checked and recorded. Note that official Beijing time is used for all timetables but local life runs roughly two hours behind it, which catches out a lot of travellers here.

ferry.note: Turpan lies in a desert depression more than 150 m below sea level in the middle of the Taklamakan region, thousands of kilometres from any coast and with no rivers or lakes of any size, so there are no passenger boat services.

full.name: Urumqi
full.blurb: Urumqi is Xinjiang's regional capital about three hours from Turpan, with the Xinjiang Regional Museum and a large bazaar district.

full.name: Tianchi (Heavenly Lake)
full.blurb: Tianchi, or Heavenly Lake, is a glacial lake in the Tian Shan mountains near Urumqi, ringed by snow-capped peaks.
